Many local places across India and Nepal claim association with the Pandavas' exile or final journey; such identifications are traditional and not historically verifiable.
Southeast Asian Versions — Java, Bali an: Old Javanese prose renderings (parwa) of books of the Mahabharata were made around the late 10th century, associated with the court of King Dharmawangsa Teguh of East Java.
The Old Javanese Kakawin Bharatayuddha, composed by Mpu Sedah and Mpu Panuluh in 1157 CE under King Jayabhaya of Kediri, retells the war in courtly verse.
Mpu Kanwa's Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (11th century, under King Airlangga) retells Arjuna's penance and his reward from the gods.

Javanese and Balinese wayang (shadow puppet and dance drama) traditions adapt the Mahabharata extensively, adding indigenous clown-servant characters (punakawan) such as Semar, Gareng, Petruk and Bagong, who have no counterpart in the Sanskrit text.

In Javanese wayang, Draupadi (Drupadi) is usually the wife of Yudhishthira (Puntadewa) alone rather than of all five brothers, and Srikandi (Shikhandi) is portrayed as a woman warrior married to Arjuna; these are major departures from the Sanskrit epic.
Southeast Asian versions should be treated as independent creative traditions, not as witnesses to an earlier Indian text.
Jain, Buddhist and Persian Tellings: Jain retellings of the Pandava and Krishna stories include Jinasena's Harivamsha Purana (783 CE), Hemachandra's Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra (12th century) and Devaprabha Suri's Pandavacharita (13th century).

In Jain tellings, Krishna is one of the nine Vasudevas of the Jain universal history; because of the violence of his life he is said to go to hell after death but is destined to become a future Tirthankara.
In Jain tellings, the Pandavas eventually become Jain monks and attain liberation, often associated with Mount Shatrunjaya, replacing the Hindu Mahaprasthanika and Svargarohana endings.

Jain versions of Krishna's end commonly have Dwaraka destroyed by fire through the wrath of an ascetic named Dvaipayana insulted by drunken Yadava youths, and Krishna killed by Jarakumara, his own half-brother; details vary between Jain authors.

Some Buddhist Jataka stories contain motifs parallel to the Mahabharata (for example, a Ghata Jataka on the fall of Vasudeva's clan and a reference to a woman with five husbands in the Kunala Jataka); their relationship to the Sanskrit epic is debated.
The Mughal emperor Akbar commissioned a Persian translation of the Mahabharata, the Razmnama ('Book of War'), in the 1580s, with illustrated manuscripts by court painters.
Modern Literary, Stage and Screen Retell: Modern Mahabharata retellings with publication dates: Rashmirathi (Dinkar, Hindi) 1952 | Andha Yug (Dharamvir Bharati, Hindi) c. 1954 | Mrityunjay (Shivaji Sawant, Marathi) 1967 | Yuganta (Irawati Karve, Marathi) 1967 | Parva (S. L. Bhyrappa, Kannada) 1979 | Randamoozham (M. T. Vasudevan Nair, Malayalam) 1984 | Yajnaseni (Pratibha Ray, Odia) 1984 | The Palace of Illusions (Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni, English) 2008

Dharamvir Bharati's Andha Yug ('The Age of Blindness') is set on the last day of the war and its aftermath, with Ashwatthama, Gandhari's curse of Krishna and Krishna's death; it is read as a meditation on post-war moral blindness after the Second World War and Partition.
S. L. Bhyrappa's Kannada novel Parva retells the epic in realistic terms, removing supernatural elements and treating the characters as historical humans.
M. T. Vasudevan Nair's Randamoozham retells the epic from Bhima's point of view, the 'second turn' of a brother who is never first.
Irawati Karve's Yuganta is a set of anthropologically informed essays on the epic's characters, notable for its unsentimental readings of Bhishma, Kunti, Gandhari, Draupadi and Karna.
Peter Brook's Mahabharata, adapted with Jean-Claude Carrière, was staged in 1985 and filmed in 1989.
B. R. Chopra's Hindi television serial Mahabharat (1988–1990) shaped popular understanding of the epic across India and includes many popular rather than Critical Edition episodes.
Karna — Sympathetic Readings: Sympathetic modern readings present Karna as a tragic hero denied his rightful status by caste prejudice and fate: abandoned at birth by Kunti, insulted as a charioteer's son at the tournament, and cursed by teachers.
Karna is celebrated for generosity (as 'Daanveer', the hero of giving), notably for giving away his natural armour and earrings to Indra disguised as a brahmin.
Karna's loyalty to Duryodhana, who made him king of Anga, and his refusal of Krishna's and Kunti's offers before the war, are central to his sympathetic portrayal.
Works central to Karna sympathy include Bhasa's Karnabhara, Ramdhari Singh Dinkar's Hindi poem Rashmirathi (1952) and Shivaji Sawant's Marathi novel Mrityunjay (1967).

Critical readings counter that Karna took part in the humiliation of Draupadi in the dice hall, urged Draupadi's disrobing and joined the group killing of Abhimanyu, so the epic portrays him as morally mixed.
The post-war revelation that Karna was the Pandavas' elder brother (Stri Parva) and Yudhishthira's grief turn the epic itself toward a retrospective sympathy for him.
Draupadi and Feminist Readings: Feminist readings highlight Draupadi's legal question in the dice hall, whether a husband who had lost himself could stake his wife, as a challenge the assembled elders could not answer.
Draupadi's speeches in the Vana Parva, criticising Yudhishthira's passivity and questioning divine justice, are read as among the epic's strongest arguments for human agency.
Draupadi's fall first on the final journey, blamed by Yudhishthira on her partiality to Arjuna, is often criticised as an unjust verdict on a woman who suffered most for the Pandavas.
Pratibha Ray's Odia novel Yajnaseni (1984) and Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni's The Palace of Illusions (2008) retell the epic from Draupadi's point of view.
Mahasweta Devi's Bengali short story 'Draupadi' (1978), translated by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1981), reimagines Draupadi as Dopdi Mejhen, a tribal woman resisting state violence.

Other women's voices discussed in feminist readings include Gandhari (who chose to blindfold herself), Kunti, Amba/Shikhandi, Madhavi (in the Udyoga Parva), Sulabha (who debates King Janaka) and the widows of the Stri Parva.
Feminist scholars disagree on whether the epic critiques patriarchy or merely displays it; readings range from Draupadi as a feminist icon to Draupadi as an instrument of male honour.
Ethics of War and Violence: The Mahabharata is widely read as a deeply ambivalent war epic: it justifies the Pandavas' war as dharmic yet shows its victory as nearly indistinguishable from defeat.

Readers debate whether Krishna's stratagems (Shikhandi, the Ashwatthama deception, the blow below the navel, Karna's death) are justified necessity, divine design beyond human ethics, or moral failures the epic deliberately exposes.
Ashwatthama's night massacre is often read as the logical end of escalating breaches of the rules of war by both sides, rather than an isolated atrocity.
The Stri Parva laments, Gandhari's curse and the golden mongoose are frequently cited as the epic's internal critique of war and royal violence.

Gandhi's allegorical reading treated the war as the inner battle between good and evil; others, including many nationalists such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, read the Gita and epic as endorsing righteous action, including force.
Modern scholars compare the epic's rules of war with just war traditions; the comparison is illuminating but anachronistic if taken as identical concepts.
Scholarly Theories of Composition: Most scholars hold that the Mahabharata grew over several centuries; a common estimate places the main period of composition between roughly the 4th century BCE and the 4th century CE.

Alf Hiltebeitel argued that the Mahabharata was composed as a written work over a relatively short span, between the mid-2nd century BCE and the turn of the Common Era; this is a minority but influential position.

The epic hints at its own growth: it calls itself 'Jaya' in its opening invocation, speaks of a 'Bharata' of 24,000 verses without the subsidiary tales, and of a full collection of 100,000 verses; the modern three-stage model (Jaya, then Bharata, then Mahabharata) is a scholarly inference from such statements, not something the text lays out.
Stated sizes of the epic in its own Adi Parva: Bharata core 24000 verses | full Mahabharata 100000 verses (traditional claims, not measured counts)

Nineteenth-century 'inversion' theories, notably by Adolf Holtzmann, claimed that the Kauravas were originally the heroes and the story was later rewritten in the Pandavas' favour; these theories are now generally rejected.
Georges Dumézil (Mythe et épopée, 1968), building on Stig Wikander (1947), read the Pandavas as reflecting Indo-European mythic functions; this comparative reading remains influential but debated.

V. S. Sukthankar's 'Bhrguization' thesis (1936) held that brahmins of the Bhrigu clan reworked and expanded the epic; Madeleine Biardeau and Alf Hiltebeitel emphasised the epic's coherent religious and mythic design.

A 6th-century copper-plate inscription from Khoh (Madhya Pradesh), commonly dated to 533–534 CE, refers to the Mahabharata as the 'collection of 100,000 verses', indicating the expanded epic existed by then.
Historicity and Dating of the War — Mult: Whether the Kurukshetra war happened is unproven; views range from a historical core in a conflict among Iron Age Kuru-Panchala clans to a largely mythic and literary creation.
Traditional Indian reckoning places the war at the junction of the Dvapara and Kali ages and dates the start of the Kali Yuga to 3102 BCE, a date used in the astronomer Aryabhata's work (499 CE).
The Aihole inscription of the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II (634 CE) dates itself 3,735 years after the Bharata war, consistent with the 3102 BCE tradition.
Another tradition, cited by Varahamihira (6th century) from Vriddha Garga and by Kalhana's Rajatarangini (12th century), places Yudhishthira about 653 years into the Kali Yuga, around 2449 BCE.

Puranic genealogies state an interval from Parikshit's birth to the coronation of Mahapadma Nanda of 1,015 or 1,050 years (manuscripts vary, some reading 1,500); scholars using this have proposed dates from around the 15th to the 9th century BCE; F. E. Pargiter proposed about 950 BCE, and B. B. Lal, using shorter average reigns, about 836 BCE.

Proposed dates for the war (all contested): Kali Yuga tradition 3102 BCE | Varahamihira/Kalhana tradition c. 2449 BCE | Puranic-genealogy estimates c. 1400–950 BCE | B. B. Lal's genealogy-plus-archaeology estimate c. 836 BCE

Archaeologist B. B. Lal's excavations at Hastinapura (1950–1952) found Painted Grey Ware levels (roughly early first millennium BCE) and evidence of a flood, which he linked with the Puranic report that the capital moved to Kaushambi after a Ganga flood; the link is suggestive, not proof.

Astronomical arguments based on planetary positions mentioned in the epic have produced widely divergent dates, for example 3067 BCE (B. N. Narahari Achar) and 5561 BCE (P. V. Vartak); most scholars regard the epic's astronomical references as internally inconsistent and unsuitable for precise dating.

Marine archaeology off Bet Dwarka and Dwarka in Gujarat (notably under S. R. Rao from the 1980s) found submerged structures that some link to the Dwaraka of the epic; dating and interpretation of these finds remain disputed.

The epic's numbers (eighteen akshauhinis, over 1.6 billion dead) and its divine interventions show that, whatever historical memory it preserves, the text is not a chronicle; precise dates should be presented as hypotheses.
